scope: Statement and four choices only, prior to author source/proof read. Separate AI reviewer, not human certification.

samples.statement: \textnormal{Let the real solution have the displayed initial data. Find the limit.}\quad x\prime=x^3-xy,\quad y\prime=-y+x^2+x^{4},\quad x(0)=\frac14,\quad y(0)=\frac1{16},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}t^{\frac{1}{4}}x(t)=?
samples.shortestRoute: Set z=y-x squared, so x prime=-xz and z prime=(-1+2x squared)z+x fourth. The ratio w=z/x fourth remains in[0,2] from the stated initial data and tends to1. Hence(x inverse fourth) prime tends to4. Global trapping and ratio convergence are essential.

samples.statement: \textnormal{For every positive integer }n,\textnormal{ let }P_n\textnormal{ be the monic polynomial of degree }n\textnormal{ satisfying the displayed equation. Its roots are listed with multiplicity. Find the limit.}\quad tP_n\prime\prime+(\frac{1}{2}n+1-t)P_n\prime+nP_n=0,\quad r_{n,1},\ldots,r_{n,n},\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac1{n+r_{n,j}}=?
samples.shortestRoute: At t=-n, the logarithmic derivative L=P prime/P is minus the resolvent. Positive roots bound its derivative by1/n, allowing the scaled polynomial ODE to give m squared+(3/2)m-1=0. Positivity selects m=1/2. Positive-root justification and uniform derivative control are essential.

samples.statement: x\prime\prime=x-x^3+\varepsilon\left[-(1+x^{2})x\prime+A\cos t\right],\qquad A>0.\textnormal{Let }x_h\textnormal{ be the positive unperturbed homoclinic orbit with its maximum at zero, and put }v_h=x_h\prime.\textnormal{Define the first-order Melnikov function by }M_A(\phi)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_h(t)\left[-(1+x_h(t)^{2})v_h(t)+A\cos(t+\phi)\right],\mathrm dt.\textnormal{Find }\inf\{A>0:M_A\textnormal{ has a simple real zero}\}.
samples.shortestRoute: The homoclinic orbit is sqrt2 sech t. Damping integral is4/3+16/15=12/5. Integrating the forcing term by parts gives sinusoidal amplitude sqrt2*pi/cosh(pi/2). A simple zero exists exactly above their ratio; at equality it is tangent.

samples.statement: y\prime\prime=6y^2+x^{3}-x^2.\textnormal{For which positive real number }a\textnormal{ does this equation admit a formal Laurent series of the displayed form, with no logarithmic terms? No convergence of the formal series is required.}\quad y(x)=(x-a)^{-2}+\sum_{j=-1}^{\infty}c_j(x-a)^j.
samples.shortestRoute: The first coefficients c minus1,c0,c1 vanish. The j4 resonance has zero multiplier j(j-1)-12 and forces f second(a)=0; for f=x cubed-x squared this gives a=1/3. All j at least5 have nonzero multipliers, proving formal extension after the free resonant coefficient.

Energy radius r satisfies r prime=-epsilon r cubed cos squared theta sin squared theta. Its averaged slow-time equation is dr/dtau=-r cubed/8, whence r1=2/sqrt5. A bounded primitive for the oscillatory zero-mean part plus Gronwall is required over times1/epsilon.

samples.statement: \textnormal{For each positive }\varepsilon,\textnormal{ let }y_\varepsilon\textnormal{ be the real solution on the negative half-line selected by the displayed asymptotic condition, continued to zero. Find the limit. The Gamma function is defined by the displayed integral.}\quad\varepsilon y_\varepsilon\prime=t^{1}+y_\varepsilon^2,\qquad \frac{y_\varepsilon(t)}{-(-t)^{\frac{1}{2}}}\longrightarrow1\quad(t\to-\infty),\qquad\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\varepsilon^{-\frac{1}{3}}y_\varepsilon(0)=?,\quad\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}e^{-u},\mathrm du\ (a>0).
samples.shortestRoute: Scale t=epsilon^(2/3)s, y=epsilon^(1/3)Y. The Riccati substitution Y=-u prime/u gives u second=-s u. The negative-root asymptotic selects u=Ai(-s), because the Bi branch gives the opposite sign. Thus Y0=Ai prime0/Ai0=-cube-root3 Gamma2/3/Gamma1/3. Ai is positive on nonnegative arguments, so continuation to0 is valid.
